pace.title: Pace
pace.definition: How long it takes you to cover one kilometer. Lower is faster.

interp.faster: That's {{diffSec}} seconds per km quicker than your four-week average.
interp.slower: That's {{diffSec}} seconds per km slower than your four-week average — terrain and how you felt both play a part.
interp.steady: Right in line with your four-week average.

gap.title: GAP (Grade Adjusted Pace)
gap.definition: Your pace converted to what it would have been on flat ground. It shows the real effort behind a hilly run.

interp.uphill: Your GAP is {{diffSec}} seconds per km quicker than your actual pace — you were climbing.
interp.downhill: Your GAP is {{diffSec}} seconds per km slower than your actual pace — the descents gave you a hand.
interp.flat: GAP and actual pace are nearly identical — this route was essentially flat.

summary.uphill: Factor in the climbing and you effectively ran {{gapPace}} per km on the flat.
summary.downhill: Take the descents out and you effectively ran {{gapPace}} per km on the flat.
summary.flat: This route was near flat, so your actual pace tells the whole story.

cadence.title: Cadence
cadence.definition: How many times your feet strike the ground each minute (spm). Taking quicker, shorter steps eases the load on your knees.

interp.low: At {{cadence}} spm you're below the {{target}} spm guideline. Try shortening your stride and turning your legs over a little faster.
interp.optimal: At {{cadence}} spm you're inside the recommended range.
interp.high: {{cadence}} spm is on the quick side — normal during intervals or downhill stretches.

rtss.title: Training Load (rTSS)
rtss.definition: How much this run asked of your body. Longer runs and harder efforts both push it up.

interp.hard: Load {{rtss}} at an intensity of {{if}} — above your threshold pace. Keep tomorrow easy, or take the day off.
interp.moderate: Load {{rtss}} at an intensity of {{if}} — a moderate effort. A day is usually enough to bounce back.
interp.easy: Load {{rtss}} at an intensity of {{if}} — an easy run. This is the kind of effort that helps you recover.

thresholdPace.title: Threshold Pace
thresholdPace.definition: The quickest pace you could hold for roughly an hour. Everything from your training zones to your load is calculated from it.

interp.set: Your target paces and training load are calculated from the threshold pace you set.
interp.unset: You haven't set one yet. Adding it sharpens both your target paces and your training load.

ctl.title: Fitness (CTL)
ctl.definition: The average training you've absorbed over the past six weeks. It climbs slowly and falls slowly.

interp.falling: Fitness {{ctl}}, easing off {{ramp}} per week — your training volume has dropped.

atl.title: Fatigue (ATL)
atl.definition: The training you've done in the last week or so. It rises fast and clears fast.

interp.high: Fatigue {{atl}} is running ahead of fitness {{ctl}} — you've been packing the sessions in.
interp.balanced: Fatigue {{atl}} and fitness {{ctl}} are nicely balanced.
interp.low: Fatigue {{atl}} sits below fitness {{ctl}} — you're resting well.

tsb.title: Form (TSB)
tsb.definition: Fitness minus fatigue. Negative means training is stacking up; positive means you've recovered.

interp.overload: TSB {{tsb}} — fatigue has piled up. Work a rest day into the week.
interp.needsRecovery: TSB {{tsb}} — a fair amount of load on board. An easy day would serve you well.
interp.productive: TSB {{tsb}} — your body is absorbing the training nicely.
interp.fresh: TSB {{tsb}} — you're well recovered. A harder session would land well.
interp.overRecovered: TSB {{tsb}} — you've rested a while. Time to start building again.

criticalPace.title: Critical Pace Curve
criticalPace.definition: The quickest pace you can sustain for each duration, drawn as a line. Short efforts sit fast; long ones settle slower.
